content.thinking:
I’ve just hit a snag: after trying to clean up stale server processes and restart, the server still seems to be binding to unexpected ports. The last two attempts to start the server resulted in it trying ports 3000, then 3001, then finally landing on 3002. When I queried the `/api/games` endpoint on port 3001, the curl returned nothing (JSON decode error), indicating that either the server isn’t listening there or the request hit some other service that returned an empty response. The subsequent attempt to check the log and fetch the games list on port 3001 also failed with the same JSON error, confirming that the server isn’t serving the API on that port.

Earlier, I added error handling to the WebSocketServer and changed the `listen` function to use a `'listening'` event instead of the callback, which should prevent duplicate banner prints. That change was applied successfully. I also attempted to kill any lingering Node processes with `pkill -f "node server/index.js"` and then restart, but the `pkill` command returned exit code 144, suggesting that it didn’t find a matching process (or permission issues). The subsequent start still reported “port 3000 busy, trying 3001, trying 3002”, meaning something else is holding those ports.

Given the pattern, it looks like there may be multiple instances of the server still running, perhaps started in previous background jobs (`nohup ... &`). The `kill %1` I used earlier only killed the most recent job in the current shell, not any other background jobs that might have been launched earlier. I need a reliable way to see which processes are listening on the 3000‑3009 range and which Node processes correspond to `server/index.js`. This will let me confirm whether stale processes are still bound to those ports and allow me to terminate them precisely.

The appropriate diagnostic command is to list all TCP listeners (`ss -tlnp`) filtered for ports 3000‑3009, and also list any running Node processes that include `server/index.js` in their command line (`pgrep -af "node server/index.js"`). Running both commands together will give a clear picture of the port occupancy and the exact PIDs I need to kill.

Thus, the next step is to execute a Bash command that does exactly that:
`ss -tlnp 2>/dev/null | grep -E ':300[0-9]' ; pgrep -af "node server/index.js"`.

This will output the listening sockets on the relevant ports and any matching Node processes, enabling me to clean up the environment before restarting the server again.
